definition: Inflame means to stir feelings, tensions, or a conflict into something hotter and more intense.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inflame. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inflame should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: One mistranslated headline inflamed a border dispute that diplomats had spent the whole summer cooling.
To provoke is merely to poke a reaction awake — weaker than inflame, which takes feeling already there and drives it into open flame.
Incense goes further than inflame: an inflamed crowd is heated and loud but can still be argued with, while an incensed one is past reasoning altogether.

To aggravate is to make an existing problem worse — any problem, with no heat required: a delay, a debt, a bad knee. Inflame is aggravation with fire in it: what worsens is feeling, and it worsens by blazing up.
To kindle is to start a small feeling gently growing — kindle an interest, a hope, a first spark of curiosity. Kindle begins; inflame takes what already burns and drives it into full flame.
To enrage is to make one person furious — the finished state of a single temper. Inflame heats a whole situation — crowds, disputes, passions — rather than tipping one person over the edge.
to calm feeling down and cool it
to drain the danger out of a tense situation

Inflame means to stir feelings, tensions, or a conflict into something hotter and more intense.
The consultant's slide — half the district labeled 'underused' — inflamed a zoning meeting that had been drowsy for an hour; by the next slide, three residents were on their feet shouting.
Inflame takes feeling that already exists and makes it blaze: irritation becomes fury, a simmering dispute boils over.
The prefix is another disguise — this in- means 'into,' not 'not.' The word is built on Latin flamma, 'flame': to inflame is to drive something into flame.
That is also why inflammable means burnable, exactly like flammable — nothing in it was ever negated, and warning labels switched to flammable to end the guessing.
Inflame nearly always makes things worse: tensions, rivalries, tempers — and, in medicine, tissue.
Aggravate worsens without heat; kindle starts a feeling small; enrage finishes one person's temper.
Passion is the exception — a speech can inflame love or ambition — but even there the word promises heat past the point of comfort.

In derby week, the radio changes that.
On Monday a talk-show host replayed a five-year-old foul on a loop and asked, with theatrical innocence, whether Southside had ever apologized.
